title: Altitude illness: what to do (descent first)
asks: how do I treat altitude sickness
do we need to go down the mountain
partner confused and stumbling at altitude
cant breathe at high camp what do I do
how far down for altitude sickness
altitude headache can I keep climbing
when is it safe to go back up after altitude sickness
can I take ibuprofen for an altitude headache
answer: Descent is the first-line and definitive treatment for nearly all altitude illness.

Confusion, loss of coordination or changes in consciousness (possible HACE), or shortness of breath at rest (possible HAPE): descend immediately and rapidly. Getting to the lowest possible altitude by the fastest means is the highest priority until symptoms fully resolve.
With possible HAPE, the person should descend with as little exertion as possible, ideally by vehicle. If they must walk, take any load off them.
Seek evacuation to medical care at a lower altitude as quickly as possible. HACE and HAPE are medical emergencies, and both require evacuation.
Have the person rest and give oxygen if it is available, but do not delay descent or evacuation for oxygen or any other treatment.
Keep the person warm with blankets and insulating layers: cold can make symptoms worse.
Keep the person calm and reassure them: stress and anxiety can make symptoms worse.

Mild acute mountain sickness only (headache with nausea, fatigue or lightheadedness, none of the signs above): stop ascending and rest at the current altitude for 1 to 2 days, with constant monitoring. Ibuprofen or acetaminophen at the usual headache dose can be used for the headache.
Avoid dehydration by drinking guided by thirst. Overhydration and forced drinking have not been shown to help.
If mountain sickness is higher risk or more severe, go down: symptoms typically resolve after a descent of 300 to 1,000 meters. The more severe it is, the more urgent the descent.
Go up again only once free of symptoms, and then no faster than 500 meters per day.
Medicines such as dexamethasone or nifedipine: their use should be determined by a medical professional.
warnings: HACE and HAPE lead to high mortality: treatment and evacuation efforts should be aggressive.
Untreated mountain sickness increases the risk of HACE.

quotes.text: Descent: This is the first line and the definitive treatment of nearly all HAI. Symptoms of AMS will typically resolve after descent of 300 - 1000 m from altitude of symptom onset. With increasing severity more urgent descent is advised. (See Appendix A.) With isolated AMS without progression to HACE or HAPE, individuals can be treated with arrest of ascent and rest at their current altitude for 1-2 days. Ascent may be resumed, at a rate no greater than 500m per day, once the individual is asymptomatic.
Mild AMS can be treated in place with constant monitoring and re-evaluation. Higher risk AMS should be evacuated to lower altitude with repeat evaluations.
Ibuprofen/Acetaminophen: Ibuprofen and acetaminophen can be used to treat headache symptoms of AMS at their usual dosing for headache therapy.
Descent: HACE leads to high mortality and morbidity. Descent to the lowest possible altitude in the most expeditious manner should be of the highest priority until symptoms fully resolve.

Descent: HAPE leads to high mortality and morbidity; thus, descent to lowest possible altitude in the most expeditious manner should be of the highest priority until symptoms fully resolve. Individuals suffering from HAPE should descend using as little exertion to themselves as possible, ideally via vehicle. If they must walk themselves, then remove any burdening load.
Oxygen: If available, oxygen should be given continuously, titrating to an SpO2>90%. Rapid evacuation should not be delayed for oxygen therapy.

Use pharmaceuticals and adjuncts listed above to begin treating HACE while coordinating evacuation. Do not delay evacuation for the aforementioned therapies. Treatment and evacuation efforts should be aggressive.
Thus, dehydration should be avoided and guided by thirst and appropriate urine output. Overhydration and forced hydration has not been shown to be helpful.
While at altitude, continue to reassess for AMS, considering differentials that may mimic AMS. Untreated AMS increases risk of HACE, whether AMS is diagnosed or not.

Immediate Descent. The most critical first aid measure for HACE is an immediate and rapid descent to lower altitudes. Descending to a lower elevation is essential to reduce the impact of high altitude on the brain.

Immediate Descent. The most critical first aid measure for HAPE is an immediate descent to lower altitudes. Every effort should be made to get the affected individual to a lower elevation as quickly as possible, as this is the most effective way to alleviate symptoms.

Rest and Oxygen. Ensure the person rests and provide supplemental oxygen if available. Oxygen therapy can help improve oxygen levels in the blood and alleviate breathing difficulties. • Keep Warm. Maintain the person's warmth by using blankets and insulating layers. Cold temperatures can exacerbate symptoms, so preventing hypothermia is important. • Stay Hydrated. Encourage the individual to drink fluids to stay hydrated. Dehydration can worsen the condition, so maintaining adequate fluid intake is essential.

Monitor Neurological Symptoms. Keep a close watch on the person's neurological symptoms. Signs of severe neurological impairment, such as confusion, loss of coordination, or changes in consciousness, require urgent medical attention. • Evacuation. Seek evacuation to an MTF at a lower altitude as quickly as possible. HACE is a medical emergency, and professional medical help should be sought without delay. • Reassure and calm. Keep the affected individual calm and reassure them. Stress and anxiety can exacerbate symptoms, so a supportive and calming environment is beneficial.
In a few Soldiers, AMS can progress to life threatening HACE or HAPE, both of which require evacuation.
HAPE is a medical emergency, and prompt action is crucial. While these first aid measures can provide initial assistance, professional medical help should be sought without delay.

Administer Medications (if available). In some cases, medications such as nifedipine or sildenafil may be used to help manage HAPE symptoms. The medical professional should determine the availability and use of these medications.

Administer Medications (if available). In some cases, medications such as dexamethasone may be used to help manage HACE symptoms. Medical professionals should determine the use of medications, and access to such medications may be limited in remote mountainous areas.

The symptoms are dyspnea at rest, cough, decreased exercise tolerance or weakness, and chest tightness or congestion. The earliest symptoms are commonly decreased exercise tolerance and dyspnea at rest.
Acute Mountain Sickness Diagnosis Criteria at altitude (2500M or higher) Headache plus at least one of these: Weakness/lightheadedness Nausea/vomiting Anorexia Fatigue

conflict: DRINKING: ATP 4-02.11 (2026) lists 'encourage the individual to drink fluids to stay hydrated' as first aid for HAPE and HACE with no condition on alertness; JTS Altitude Emergencies 2024 says avoid dehydration guided by thirst and that overhydration and forced hydration have not been shown to help. The card keeps drinking as a thirst-guided line after the mild-sickness step and does not tell rescuers to give drinks to a confused or drowsy person. DESCEND OR STAY for mild mountain sickness: JTS says mild AMS can be treated in place with rest for 1-2 days and constant monitoring, higher-risk AMS should be evacuated lower; ATP 3-50.21 (2018) and ATP 4-02.11 name descent, rest and hydration without a stay-in-place option. MEDICINES (acetazolamide, dexamethasone, nifedipine doses) are given only in JTS for medical providers and are left off the card. HHS Ship's Medicine Chest 2003 and FEMA P-2064 (2020) have nothing on altitude illness.

review.notes: Confirmed in context: JTS (descent first and definitive; 300-1000 m; urgent with severity; mild AMS rest 1-2 days with monitoring; resume at no more than 500 m/day once symptom-free; HACE/HAPE descent to lowest altitude fastest; HAPE minimal exertion, vehicle, remove load; oxygen without delaying evacuation; ibuprofen/acetaminophen at usual dose; drink to thirst), ATP 4-02.11 (immediate descent, rest and oxygen, warmth, reassurance, evacuation, medicines by professionals), TB MED 508 (evacuation). Order is right (descent first). Drinking and stay-or-descend disagreements are listed; the card does not tell anyone to give drinks to a confused person. Named drugs present. No PDF junk. Recommended, not blocking: when descent is impossible (night, weather), JTS says a portable hyperbaric chamber, if carried, buys time ('a temporary stopgap'); a one-line 'if you cannot descend' with oxygen, hyperbaric bag, warmth and rest would close the (c) gap. JTS lists respiratory depressants as a HAPE risk; consider 'no sleeping pills or alcohol' only if a quote supports it.
